blocks.content: Abstract
blocks.label: Text

blocks.content: The Boolean lattice  \( BL_{n}, n \geq 3 \) , is the graph whose vertex set is the collection of all subsets of  \( [n] = \{1, 2, \ldots, n\} \) , where two subsets U and W are adjacent if and only if their symmetric difference has precisely one element. In the graph  \( BL_{n} \) , the layer  \( L_{k} \)  is the family of all k-element subsets of  \( [n] \) . The subgraph  \( BL_{n}(k - 1, k) \)  is the induced subgraph of  \( BL_{n} \)  on layers  \( L_{k-1} \)  and  \( L_{k} \) . This graph is bipartite and, when n = 2k - 1, is k-regular and isomorphic to the bipartite double cover  \( 2 \cdot O_{k} \)  of the odd graph  \( O_{k} \) . In this paper, we determine the full adjacency spectrum—eigenvalues together with their multiplicities—of the line graph  \( L(BL_{n}(k-1, k)) \)  for all admissible values of n and k. As a consequence, we show that  \( L(BL_{n}(k-1, k)) \)  is an integral graph whenever n = 2k - 1, and we recover as a special case the spectrum of the line graph  \( L(n) \)  of  \( BL_{n}(1, 2) \)  established by Mirafzal [13].

blocks.content: 1 Introduction
blocks.label: Text

blocks.content: Background and motivation
blocks.label: Text

blocks.content: Spectral graph theory—the study of graphs through the eigenvalues and eigenvectors of their associated matrices—is one of the most active areas of algebraic combinatorics. The adjacency spectrum of a graph encodes a wealth of structural information: it governs expansion properties, random walk mixing times, the existence of perfect matchings, and chromatic properties, among many other things. A comprehensive account of the classical theory can be found in the monographs of Brouwer and Haemers [5] and Godsil and Royle [9].
blocks.label: Text

blocks.content: Among the most studied graph families in this context are distance-regular graphs, which include the Johnson graphs  \( J(n,k) \) , the Hamming graphs, the Kneser graphs, the odd graphs  \( O_{k} \) , and the hypercube  \( Q_{n} \) . Their spectra are completely determined by their intersection arrays, and a rich combinatorial theory has been developed for them; see Brouwer, Cohen, and Neumaier [4] for a comprehensive treatment. In recent years, considerable attention has shifted to graphs derived from these classical families—their line graphs, square graphs, subdivision graphs, and bipartite doubles—and to determining the spectra of these derived graphs.
blocks.label: Text

blocks.content: Integral graphs
blocks.label: Text

blocks.content: A graph  \( \Gamma \)  is called integral if all eigenvalues of its adjacency matrix are integers. The concept was introduced by Harary and Schwenk [10] in 1974, who raised the question of characterizing all integral graphs. Despite several decades of effort, a complete classification remains elusive, and the search for new infinite families of integral graphs is an active line of research.
blocks.label: Text

blocks.content: Watanabe and Schwenk in [16] proved that a tree is integral if and only if it belongs to a specific finite set. Bussemaker, Cvetković [6], and Schwenk [15] independently classified cubic integral graphs, finding exactly 13 non-isomorphic examples. The study was extended to 4-regular graphs by Cvetković, Simić, and Stevanović in [8], who identified 1998 possible spectra for 4-regular bipartite integral graphs; see also the work of Ahmadi et al. [2]. A significant source of infinite families of integral graphs is furnished by Cayley graphs: Abdollahi and Vatandoost [1] characterized which Cayley graphs over abelian groups are integral, and subsequent work has produced integral Cayley graphs over many non-abelian groups. We refer to the monograph [5] and the references therein for a broader survey.
blocks.label: Text

In other words,  \( BL_{n} \)  is the n-dimensional hypercube  \( Q_{n} \) , where vertices are identified with binary strings of length n via characteristic vectors of subsets. In the graph  \( BL_{n} \) , the layer  \( L_{k} \)  is the family of all k-element subsets of [n]. The induced subgraph  \( BL_{n}(k-1,k) \)  on layers  \( L_{k-1} \)  and  \( L_{k} \)  is a bipartite graph with vertex bipartition  \( V_{1} \cup V_{2} \) , where

\]

blocks.content: These bipartite layer graphs enjoy rich structural properties. By [14], the graph \( BL_{n}(k - 1,k) \) is isomorphic to the consecutive-layer graph \( Q_{n}(k - 1,k) \) of the hypercube. Furthermore, as shown by Cao, Lv, and Wang [7], for \( n \geq k \) the graph \( BL_{n}(k - 1,k) \) is isomorphic to the doubled Johnson graph \( J(n,k - 1,k) \).
blocks.label: Text

blocks.content: Line graphs and their spectra
blocks.label: Text

blocks.content: Recall that the line graph  \( L(\Gamma) \)  of a graph  \( \Gamma \)  is the graph whose vertices are the edges of  \( \Gamma \), two vertices of  \( L(\Gamma) \)  being adjacent whenever the corresponding edges of  \( \Gamma \)  share an endpoint. A fundamental relationship between a graph and its line graph is given by the identity  \( B^{T}B = A(L(\Gamma)) + 2I \), where B is the incidence matrix of  \( \Gamma \); this makes it possible to read off the spectrum of  \( L(\Gamma) \)  from the singular values of B. Line graphs of bipartite graphs always have -2 as an eigenvalue, and by the Perron–Frobenius theorem, the largest eigenvalue of  \( L(\Gamma) \)  equals  \( \Delta(\Gamma) + \delta(\Gamma) - 2 \)  when  \( \Gamma \)  is biregular.
blocks.label: Text

blocks.content: The spectra of line graphs of classical combinatorial graphs have attracted sustained attention. The line graph of the complete graph  \( K_{n} \)  is the triangular graph  \( T(n) \) , whose spectrum is classical. Mirafzal [13] introduced the family  \( H(n) = \)
blocks.label: Text

blocks.content: \( BL_{n}(1,2) \)  and showed that its line graph  \( L(n) \)  is a vertex-transitive integral graph with exactly five distinct eigenvalues n-1, n-2, 0, -1, -2; however, the multiplicities of these eigenvalues were left undetermined in [13]. Mirafzal also studied algebraic properties of line graphs arising from consecutive layers of the hypercube in [14], where it is shown that these line graphs are Cayley graphs under certain conditions. More recently, Mirafzal [12] established that the line graph of the crown graph is distance-integral, and Kogani and Mirafzal [11] determined the distance spectrum of a broader class of distance-integral graphs. These results reflect a general trend of deriving spectral properties of derived graphs from those of well-understood base graphs.
blocks.label: Text

blocks.content: Contribution of this paper
blocks.label: Text

blocks.content: In this paper, we determine the complete adjacency spectrum of the line graph  \( L(BL_{n}(k-1,k)) \)  for all  \( n \geq 2k-1 \) . Since  \( BL_{n}(k-1,k) \cong BL_{n}(n-k,n-k+1) \) , we may assume without loss of generality that  \( n \geq 2k-1 \) . Our approach rests on two key observations: (i) the spectrum of  \( BL_{n}(k-1,k) \)  can be deduced from that of the Johnson graph  \( J(n,k-1) \) , and (ii) the spectrum of the line graph  \( L(BL_{n}(k-1,k)) \)  can then be extracted from the nonzero singular values of the incidence matrix B of  \( BL_{n}(k-1,k) \)  via Lemma 2.1.
blocks.label: Text

blocks.content: More precisely, we obtain the following. When  \( n \geq 2k \) , the eigenvalues of  \( L(BL_{n}(k-1,k)) \)  are integers and their multiplicities are expressed in terms of binomial coefficients (Theorem 3.2). When n = 2k - 1, the graph  \( BL_{n}(k-1,k) \)  is itself a distance-transitive regular graph, and its line graph is vertex-transitive with an entirely integral spectrum; we determine this spectrum completely in Theorem 3.4. As a special case (Example 3.3), we recover and complete the spectrum of  \( L(n) \)  left open by Mirafzal in [13]: the multiplicities of the distinct eigenvalues  \( n-1, n-2, 0, -1, -2 \)  of  \( L(n) \)  are 1, n-1,  \( \frac{n(n-3)}{2} \) , n-1, and  \( \frac{(n-1)(n-2)}{2} \) , respectively.
blocks.label: Text

blocks.content: Notation and adjacency spectra
blocks.label: Text

blocks.content: The adjacency matrix  \( A(\Gamma) \)  of a graph  \( \Gamma \)  is the symmetric  \( \{0,1\} \) -matrix whose rows and columns are indexed by  \( V(\Gamma) \) , with the  \( (i,j) \) -entry equal to 1 if  \( \{i,j\}\in E(\Gamma) \)  and 0 otherwise. The eigenvalues of  \( \Gamma \)  are the roots of the characteristic polynomial  \( \det(xI_{n}-A(\Gamma)) \) . The spectrum of  \( \Gamma \)  is the multiset of eigenvalues of  \( A(\Gamma) \) . When the distinct eigenvalues are  \( \lambda_{1}>\lambda_{2}>\cdots>\lambda_{r} \)  with respective multiplicities  \( m_{1},m_{2},\ldots,m_{r} \) , we write
blocks.label: Text

blocks.content:
\[
\mathrm{Spec} (\Gamma) = \left\{\lambda_ {1} ^ {m _ {1}}, \lambda_ {2} ^ {m _ {2}}, \ldots , \lambda_ {r} ^ {m _ {r}} \right\}.
\]
blocks.label: Formula

blocks.content: The graph \(\Gamma\) is called integral if all eigenvalues belong to \(\mathbb{Z}\). Integral graphs form a distinguished class with applications in coding theory, quantum walks, and network
blocks.label: Text

blocks.content: design; see [1, 2, 10] and the references therein for recent developments.

blocks.content: 2 Definitions and Preliminaries
blocks.label: Text

blocks.content: All graphs in this paper are assumed to be finite, simple, and connected. We follow standard notation from [9] for concepts not defined here. The incidence matrix \( B \) of a graph \( \Gamma \) is the \( \{0,1\} \)-matrix with rows indexed by vertices and columns indexed by edges, such that the \( (i,j) \)-entry equals 1 if and only if vertex \( i \) is an endpoint of edge \( j \). If \( \Gamma \) has \( n \) vertices and \( e \) edges, then \( B \) has order \( n \times e \).
blocks.label: Text

blocks.content: The rank of the incidence matrix has a clean combinatorial description: if  \( \Gamma \)  is a graph with n vertices and  \( c_{0} \)  bipartite connected components, then  \( \text{rank}(B) = n - c_{0} \) . In particular, if  \( \Gamma \)  is a connected bipartite graph with n vertices, then  \( \text{rank}(B) = n - 1 \) .
blocks.label: Text

blocks.content: The line graph of a graph \(\Gamma\) is the graph \(L(\Gamma)\) whose vertex set is \(E(\Gamma)\), with two edges of \(\Gamma\) being adjacent in \(L(\Gamma)\) if and only if they share an endpoint in \(\Gamma\).
blocks.label: Text

blocks.content: Lemma 2.1 ([9]) Let \( B \) be the incidence matrix of the graph \( \Gamma \) on \( n \) vertices and \( m \) edges, and let \( L \) be the line graph of \( \Gamma \). Then \( B^T B = A(L) + 2I_m \), where \( A(L) \) is the adjacency matrix of the line graph of \( \Gamma \).
blocks.label: Text

blocks.content: Lemma 2.2 ([9]) Let \( B \) be the incidence matrix of the graph \( \Gamma \) on \( n \) vertices and \( m \) edges. Then \( BB^{T} = \Delta(\Gamma) + A(\Gamma) \), where \( \Delta(\Gamma) \) is the diagonal \( n \times n \) matrix whose ii-entry is equal to the degree of vertex \( i \).

blocks.content: 4 Conclusion
blocks.label: Text

blocks.content: In this paper, we have determined the complete adjacency spectrum of the line graph  \( L(BL_{n}(k-1,k)) \)  for all integers  \( k \geq 2 \)  and  \( n \geq 2k - 1 \) . Our main contributions are as follows.
blocks.label: Text

blocks.content: - In Theorem 3.1, we computed the spectrum of the bipartite layer graph \( BL_{n}(k - 1,k) \) for \( n \geq 2k - 1 \), expressing the eigenvalues and their multiplicities via those of the Johnson graph \( J(n,k - 1) \).
blocks.label: Text

blocks.content: - In Theorem 3.2 (the case \( n \geq 2k \)), we showed that all eigenvalues of \( L(BL_n(k - 1,k)) \) are integers, and we gave explicit formulas for eigenvalues and their multiplicities in terms of binomial coefficients.
blocks.label: Text

blocks.content: - In Theorem 3.4 (the case \( n = 2k - 1 \)), where \( BL_{n}(k - 1,k) \cong 2 \cdot O_{k} \), we established the complete integral spectrum of the vertex-transitive line graph \( L(BL_{n}(k - 1,k)) \).
blocks.label: Text

blocks.content: - As a special case (Example 3.3), we completed the result of Mirafzal [13] by computing the multiplicities of all eigenvalues of the line graph \( L(n) = L(BL_n(1,2)) \), which were left undetermined in [13].
blocks.label: Text

blocks.content: These results show that the line graphs  \( L(BL_{n}(k-1,k)) \)  constitute a rich infinite family of integral graphs accessible through combinatorial methods. Several natural questions remain open. For instance, one may ask whether  \( L(BL_{n}(k-1,k)) \)  is determined by its spectrum—that is, whether a graph with the same spectrum must be isomorphic to  \( L(BL_{n}(k-1,k)) \) . Another direction is to determine the distance spectrum of these line graphs, extending the distance-integral results of Mirafzal [12] and Kogani–Mirafzal [11] to the present family. We hope that the techniques introduced here will be useful in these and related investigations.
